extracted.intended_audience: fans and researchers of television comedy and roast production
extracted.subtask_short: Comedy Central roast format and norms
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the format, production practices, content limits, editing decisions, recurring personnel, venues, international versions, and reception metrics for the Comedy Central Roast series of celebrity roast specials. Useful for understanding how a televised roast is produced and evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series format — number of roasters and sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Eight to ten people are invited, and they each roast one another before finally roasting the titular subject of the roast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The network typically airs one or two roasts every year; the format includes multiple roasters who alternate sets and culminate in roasting the roastee. Examples throughout the article list roaster lineups for each roast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running time
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard running time for the Comedy Central Roast specials is listed as 90 minutes; this constrains show pacing and how many sets/segments can fit into a broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roastee topic restrictions (off-limits requests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some roastees have stated that certain topics are off limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pamela Anderson prohibited jokes about her Hepatitis C infection; Joan Rivers disallowed jokes about her daughter Melissa; William Shatner asked that the death of his wife not be mentioned; Donald Trump prohibited jokes about him not being as wealthy as he claims. Producers and roasters often respect or negotiate these requests prior to taping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roastees who impose no limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Others have imposed no limits on the topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: David Hasselhoff is cited as having imposed no limits. This informs how writers and performers approach material for a given roast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and broadcast cuts for sensitivity or at performers' request
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes or segments have been removed from the final broadcast for sensitivity or at performers' requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Steve-O's Station nightclub fire joke was removed on his request; a Lenny Clarke Bill Hicks cigarette gag was cut; Jeff Ross' joke referencing the Aurora massacre was not in the broadcast; multiple Paul Walker jokes at the Justin Bieber roast were cut. Producers and network editors trim material post-taping for content sensitivity and audience standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing for legal and rights reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Content may be edited or omitted for legal reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Clips from Two and a Half Men (Charlie Sheen's tenure) were not used in a montage for legal reasons. Legal clearance can determine what archival material or clips appear in the televised roast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-taped and surprise guest appearances as a production device
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts often include pre-taped appearances and surprise guest appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists many pre-taped segments and surprise guest cameos (e.g., Michael J. Fox, Peter Gallagher, Leonard Nimoy pre-taped or surprise appearances). These elements are used to vary pacing and add production value beyond live roaster sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and recurrence of roastmasters and recurring roasters
rubrics_metrics.description: A roastmaster leads the event and certain roasters recur across roasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article marks roastmasters (RM) and notes frequent roasters (Jeff Ross has appeared in most roasts, Seth MacFarlane as the most frequent roastmaster). Assigning a roastmaster and booking recurring performers are part of the series' production conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone spectrum — from intentionally shocking/racy to tame/cheesy approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Roast material varies in tone; performers may choose shocking/racy material or intentionally tame/cheesy jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Norm Macdonald's set avoided racy content and used intentionally cheesy, antiquated jokes despite being asked to be 'shocking.' Conversely, other roasts feature racy sexual jokes, biting insults, and deliberately provocative material. Tone choice affects audience reaction and editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and performer reaction influences editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience reaction and later criticism can lead to edits or shape future editing choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ann Coulter's set received booing and later discussion about editing to change perceptions; complaints or poor reception (e.g., Mike 'The Situation' widely panned) have prompted Comedy Central to pull or edit jokes from airings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production elements — montages, musical backing, and grand entrances
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts use production elements like montages, background music, and grand entrances for the roastee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A montage with background music was used for William Shatner; Charlie Sheen entered riding a replica locomotive. These staging choices enhance spectacle but may be edited differently for DVD vs broadcast releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue selection and filming locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts are filmed at particular venues and studios that are reused across multiple roasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of the Alec Baldwin roast, Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City hosted the most roasts. Venue choice (studio vs ballroom) influences staging, audience size, and production logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: International adaptations and local roasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2010, Comedy Central affiliates outside the United States have occasionally produced their own roasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twelve such international roasts have aired in five countries; the article lists roasts from Africa, Latin America, Netherlands, New Zealand, Spain, etc. Local versions adapt the roast format to regional sensibilities and talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success metrics — viewership numbers and awards/nominations
rubrics_metrics.description: Roast success is measured by viewership and industry recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists US viewers (millions) for each roast and notes awards such as a 2007 Primetime Emmy nomination (Outstanding Variety Special for the William Shatner roast). Ratings and awards are used to evaluate a roast's impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancelled or rescheduled roasts due to logistical or negotiation issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts may be cancelled or replaced due to scheduling, location demands, or other disagreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Willie Nelson's planned roast was cancelled; Kid Rock's roast was replaced because he insisted it be filmed in Detroit, which Comedy Central refused. Planning constraints and talent conditions can derail or reschedule planned roasts.
